h1: Returnable glass bottles in Indian beer and why they matter to cost
title: Returnable Beer Bottles in India | Craft Beer School
desc: How returnable glass bottles work in Indian beer, from collection and washing to breakage and trips. Why they matter so much to cost.
teaser: That 650 ml bottle in your hand has probably been filled before. Possibly many times. Here is why that matters to the cost sheet.
standfirst: Much of India's mainstream beer goes into glass bottles that come back, get washed and get filled again. For finance, procurement and supply teams the returnable bottle is one of the biggest and least visible levers in beer cost.
sections: A bottle that travels in a loop

A new glass bottle is one of the most expensive single items in the cost of a bottle of beer before tax. A returnable system spreads that cost across many fills.

The loop runs like this. Beer is filled and sold. Empty bottles are collected by shops, bars, scrap dealers and aggregators, then bought back and returned to the brewery in crates or bags. The brewery inspects them, washes them, fills them and sends them out again. Bottles that are chipped, badly scuffed, dirty beyond cleaning or the wrong shape are rejected along the way.

In India the 650 ml amber bottle is the backbone of this system. Many brewers use bottles of a similar standard shape, so empties from one brand can end up in another brand's line, with embossing and labels sorting out who owns what.

Returned bottles go through a bottle washer before they see beer again. This is a long tunnel machine that soaks bottles in hot caustic soda solution, strips off old labels and rinses them in stages. The caustic bath typically runs at around 70 to 80 °C, hot and strong enough to remove dried beer residue, glue and microbes.

After washing, an empty bottle inspector checks each one with cameras for cracks, chips, residue and foreign objects. Rejects are broken up for recycling. The survivors go to the filler.

All of that costs money: caustic, water, steam, power, labour, label pulp disposal and the maintenance of a large machine. Those costs are part of the price of every reuse.
The number that drives the economics

The key figure is trippage: how many times, on average, a bottle is filled before it is lost or rejected. The cost of a bottle per fill is roughly the purchase price divided by the number of trips, plus the cost of collection, washing and inspection for each trip.

A few things push trippage down:

  • Bottles that do not come back because collection is weak in an area.
  • Breakage in handling, transport and at the outlet.
  • Scuffing, the white rings where bottles rub together, which eventually makes them look shabby enough to reject.
  • Bottles diverted into other uses or lost to other brands.

Small changes in trippage move cost per litre noticeably. That is why the bottle pool gets so much attention in brewery finance meetings. Our guide to beer cost of goods shows where glass sits alongside malt, excise and energy.

Returnable glass touches several lines that are easy to miss:

  • Working capital. The bottle float, bottles in the market, in depots and in the brewery, is a large pool of money tied up in glass.
  • Buyback price. What the brewery pays for empties changes how many come back. Pay too little and collection weakens. Pay too much and margin suffers.
  • Accounting. Companies treat returnable bottles in different ways, as assets depreciated over their expected life or as a cost per fill. Your company's policy shapes how bottle cost appears in reports, so ask your controller rather than assuming.
  • New glass purchases. When trippage drops, new glass orders rise, often at short notice and at higher prices before peak season.
Where returnables meet the supply chain

Returnables make logistics two-way. Trucks that take full bottles out should ideally bring empties back. Depots need space for crates of empties as well as full stock. Before summer, breweries build up a stock of clean empties so filling does not stall when demand peaks. A shortage of empties can limit how much beer a brewery can pack, whatever the tank capacity says. The wider flow is covered in the beer supply chain explained.

Cans and single-use glass avoid the reverse loop but cost more per pack and generate waste that has to be collected for recycling. Our guide to kegs versus cans covers that trade-off.
Safety and quality are part of the cost

A returnable bottle that has been scuffed and stressed over many trips is more likely to fail under the pressure of carbonated beer. Inspection and rejection are a safety measure as well as a quality one. Washing failures can leave residue that shows up as a customer complaint. Both have a cost that never appears on the glass invoice.

For a new joiner the simplest way to understand all this is to stand next to a bottle washer and an empty bottle inspector for twenty minutes. The reject bin tells you more about trippage than any spreadsheet.
faqs: How many times is a beer bottle reused in India?
It varies widely by brewer and region, depending on collection, breakage and rejection rates. Companies track their own average, called trippage.
Yes, when the system works as designed. Bottles are washed in hot caustic solution, rinsed and inspected by machine before refilling. Damaged bottles are rejected.
Why do some bottles have white rings?
Those are scuff marks from bottles rubbing against each other on lines and in crates over many trips. Heavy scuffing is one reason bottles get rejected.
